sectionTitle: Synthetic and naturally occurring polymers (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Alkenes can be used to make polymers such as poly(ethene) and poly(propene) by addition polymerisation.
In addition polymerisation reactions, many small molecules (monomers) join together to form very large molecules (polymers).
For example:
In addition polymers the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer because no other molecule is formed in the reaction.
Students should be able to:
recognise addition polymers and monomers from diagrams in the forms shown and from the presence of the functional group C=C in the monomers
draw diagrams to represent the formation of a polymer from a given alkene monomer
relate the repeating unit to the monomer.

Condensation polymerisation involves monomers with two functional groups. When these types of monomers react they join together, usually losing small molecules such as water, and so the reactions are called condensation reactions.
The simplest polymers are produced from two different monomers with two of the same functional groups on each monomer.
For example:
ethanediol
and
hexanedioic acid
polymerise to produce a polyester:
Students should be able to explain the basic principles of condensation polymerisation by reference to the functional groups in the monomers and the repeating units in the polymers.
Amino acids have two different functional groups in a molecule. Amino acids react by condensation polymerisation to produce polypeptides.
For example: glycine is H₂ NCH₂ COOH and polymerises to produce the polypeptide
Different amino acids can be combined in the same chain to produce proteins.
DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a large molecule essential for life. DNA encodes genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.

Most DNA molecules are two polymer chains, made from four different monomers called nucleotides, in the form of a double helix. Other naturally occurring polymers important for life include proteins, starch and cellulose.
Students should be able to name the types of monomers from which these naturally occurring polymers are made.

concepts.definition: A small molecule that joins with many others of the same or a different kind to build a polymer. For addition polymerisation the monomer must contain a C=C double bond.
A very large molecule made when many small monomer molecules join together in a long chain.
A reaction in which many alkene monomers join together to form a polymer, and no other product is formed.
The addition polymer made from ethene, CH₂=CH₂. Its repeating unit is –CH₂–CH₂–.
The addition polymer made from propene, CH₃CH=CH₂. Its repeating unit is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–.
The section of a polymer chain that repeats over and over. In an addition polymer it contains exactly the same atoms as the monomer, with the C=C replaced by a C–C single bond.
The carbon–carbon double bond. Its presence in a molecule shows that the molecule is an alkene and can act as a monomer for addition polymerisation.
The bonds drawn through the brackets of a repeating unit. They show that the unit is joined to further units on both sides in a long chain.
The symbol used for the large number of monomer molecules that react, and for the equally large number of repeating units in the polymer chain formed.
A reaction in which monomers that each carry two functional groups join together, usually losing a small molecule such as water each time a link is made.
The group of atoms in a molecule that decides how that molecule reacts, for example –OH, –COOH, –NH₂ or C=C.
A monomer with two carbon atoms carrying an –OH group on each of them, HOCH₂CH₂OH. It supplies the alcohol groups in a polyester.
A monomer with six carbon atoms carrying a –COOH group at each end, HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH. It supplies the acid groups in a polyester.
The link formed when an –OH group and a –COOH group react and a molecule of water is lost. Many ester links along a chain make a polyester.
The condensation polymer formed when a diol and a dicarboxylic acid, such as ethanediol and hexanedioic acid, polymerise together with the loss of water.
A molecule containing two different functional groups, an amino group –NH₂ and a carboxyl group –COOH. Glycine is H₂NCH₂COOH.
The condensation polymer formed when many amino acid molecules join together, losing a molecule of water at each link.
A naturally occurring polymer built from different amino acids combined in the same chain.
Deoxyribonucleic acid, a large molecule essential for life that encodes the genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.
The monomer from which DNA is built. Four different nucleotides are used, and most DNA molecules are two chains of them in a double helix.
The shape taken by most DNA molecules, in which two polymer chains are twisted around one another.
A naturally occurring polymer made from glucose monomers, used by plants as an energy store.
A naturally occurring polymer, also made from glucose monomers, that forms plant cell walls.
A polymer made by living things rather than in industry. Examples important for life are DNA, proteins, starch and cellulose.

misconceptions.question: Which molecule is the monomer for poly(ethene)?
misconceptions.correct: Ethene, CH₂=CH₂, which contains a C=C double bond.
misconceptions.misconception: Poly(ethene) is made from ethane, because ethane is the familiar two-carbon hydrocarbon and the names sound the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Ethene' and 'ethane' differ by one letter and sound almost identical when spoken, and alkanes are taught first.
misconceptions.correction: Only alkenes make addition polymers. Ethane, C₂H₆, has only single bonds, so nothing can open up and it cannot polymerise.

misconceptions.question: Why can alkanes not be used as monomers for addition polymerisation?
misconceptions.correct: They are saturated: every bond is a single bond, so no bond can open to join molecules together.
misconceptions.misconception: Saturated molecules join together easily because being 'saturated' means they are full and ready to react.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Saturated' sounds like 'full', which students read as reactive or complete, rather than as having no double bond.
misconceptions.correction: Saturated means the molecule already holds as many hydrogen atoms as possible and has no C=C to open, so it cannot add on to another molecule.

misconceptions.question: Is a small molecule released during addition polymerisation?
misconceptions.correct: No. The polymer is the only product.
misconceptions.misconception: Addition polymerisation releases a water molecule each time two monomers join.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Condensation polymerisation is met soon afterwards, and water loss is the memorable detail, so it gets attached to both types.
misconceptions.correction: In addition polymerisation nothing else is formed, which is exactly why the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer.

misconceptions.question: Does the repeating unit of an addition polymer still contain C=C?
misconceptions.correct: No. The double bond opens and becomes a single C–C bond in the chain.
misconceptions.misconception: The repeating unit keeps the C=C double bond, since the monomer had one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students copy the monomer straight into the brackets without changing the bond, because the atoms are unchanged.
misconceptions.correction: The C=C is the bond that opens up to form the two new bonds to neighbouring units, so it can no longer be a double bond.

misconceptions.question: Does the repeating unit contain the same atoms as the monomer?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, exactly the same atoms in the same numbers.
misconceptions.misconception: Atoms are lost from the monomer as the chain forms, so the repeating unit is smaller than the monomer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students assume that joining molecules must cost something, by analogy with condensation reactions.
misconceptions.correction: No other molecule is formed, so every atom of every monomer ends up in the polymer.

misconceptions.question: What does n stand for in n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)–n ?
misconceptions.correct: A very large number of monomer molecules, and the same number of repeating units.
misconceptions.misconception: n stands for a small fixed number such as two or three.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balanced equations normally use small whole numbers, so a letter is read as standing in for one.
misconceptions.correction: A polymer chain contains thousands of repeating units; n is a large, unspecified number that is the same on both sides.

misconceptions.question: What holds the monomer units together in a polymer chain?
misconceptions.correct: Strong covalent bonds formed when the C=C opens.
misconceptions.misconception: The units are held to each other by intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Intermolecular forces are used to explain the properties of polymers, so students apply them to the chain itself.
misconceptions.correction: Within a chain the units are joined by covalent bonds; intermolecular forces act only between separate chains.

misconceptions.question: Why are bonds drawn through the brackets of a repeating unit?
misconceptions.correct: To show the unit continues into further units on both sides.
misconceptions.misconception: The brackets enclose a complete separate molecule, so no bonds should cross them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Brackets elsewhere in chemistry enclose a finished group, so students close the unit off.
misconceptions.correction: The extension bonds are part of the required diagram: they show the unit is one link in a long chain.

misconceptions.question: Are all the polymer chains in a sample the same length?
misconceptions.correct: No. Chains contain different numbers of repeating units.
misconceptions.misconception: Every chain contains exactly the same fixed number of monomer units.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formulae usually describe one fixed molecule, so students expect a polymer to have one fixed size too.
misconceptions.correction: n is not a fixed number; a sample contains chains of many different lengths, all with the same repeating unit.

misconceptions.question: Which alkene is the monomer for poly(propene)?
misconceptions.correct: Propene, CH₃CH=CH₂.
misconceptions.misconception: Poly(propene) is made from propane, because the polymer chain contains only single bonds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The finished polymer really is saturated, so students work backwards and choose the saturated starting material.
misconceptions.correction: The chain is saturated because the double bond of propene opened during polymerisation. The monomer itself must be the alkene.

misconceptions.question: What does 'condensation' mean in condensation polymerisation?
misconceptions.correct: That a small molecule, usually water, is lost as the monomers join.
misconceptions.misconception: It means a gas condenses into a liquid as the polymer is formed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The everyday meaning of condensation, from weather and windows, is far more familiar than the chemical one.
misconceptions.correction: Here condensation refers to the loss of a small molecule at each link, not to a change of state.

misconceptions.question: Do condensation monomers need a C=C double bond?
misconceptions.correct: No. They need two functional groups, such as –OH, –COOH or –NH₂.
misconceptions.misconception: All polymerisation needs a carbon–carbon double bond in the monomer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Addition polymerisation is met first and the C=C rule is drilled, so it is carried over to every polymer.
misconceptions.correction: The C=C rule belongs only to addition polymerisation. Condensation monomers react through two functional groups instead.

misconceptions.question: Can a monomer with only one functional group form a polymer?
misconceptions.correct: No. It could react once and then the chain would stop.
misconceptions.misconception: One functional group per monomer is enough to build a long chain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think about a single reaction between two molecules and do not picture the chain having to grow at both ends.
misconceptions.correction: Two functional groups are needed so that each monomer can join on both sides and the chain can keep growing.

misconceptions.question: How many –OH groups does ethanediol have?
misconceptions.correct: Two, one on each of its two carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Ethanediol has one –OH group, like ethanol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ethanol is met first and looks similar; the '-diol' ending is not read as meaning two –OH groups.
misconceptions.correction: The 'di' in ethanediol tells you there are two –OH groups, which is what allows it to link at both ends.

misconceptions.question: How many –COOH groups does hexanedioic acid have?
misconceptions.correct: Two, one at each end of the six-carbon chain.
misconceptions.misconception: Hexanedioic acid has a single –COOH group at one end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Carboxylic acids are first met as one-ended molecules such as ethanoic acid, so that picture is reused.
misconceptions.correction: The 'dioic' ending shows two –COOH groups, one at each end, so the molecule can link on both sides.

misconceptions.question: Which small molecule is lost when a polyester forms?
misconceptions.correct: Water.
misconceptions.misconception: Carbon dioxide is given off when the monomers join.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acids are associated with giving off carbon dioxide from carbonate reactions, so that product is recalled.
misconceptions.correction: The –OH and the –COOH group combine, and the atoms removed are H and OH, which form water.

misconceptions.question: Which polymer forms from ethanediol and hexanedioic acid?
misconceptions.correct: A polyester.
misconceptions.misconception: The product is a polypeptide, because a condensation reaction always makes one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both polyesters and polypeptides are condensation polymers, and the two names get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: The link depends on the groups used. –OH with –COOH gives an ester link and so a polyester; –NH₂ with –COOH gives a polypeptide.

misconceptions.question: What functional groups does an amino acid have?
misconceptions.correct: Two different groups: –NH₂ and –COOH.
misconceptions.misconception: An amino acid has two of the same functional group, like the monomers used for a polyester.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule that condensation monomers carry two of the same group is learned for polyesters and then over-applied.
misconceptions.correction: Amino acids are the exception the specification highlights: the two groups are different, which is why one monomer can polymerise alone.

misconceptions.question: Which small molecule is lost when amino acids polymerise?
misconceptions.correct: Water.
misconceptions.misconception: Ammonia is lost, because the amino group contains nitrogen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The –NH₂ group is visible in the formula, so students expect the nitrogen-containing molecule to leave.
misconceptions.correction: The nitrogen stays in the chain. The H from –NH₂ and the OH from –COOH leave together as water.

misconceptions.question: What makes a protein different from a simple polypeptide?
misconceptions.correct: Different amino acids are combined in the same chain.
misconceptions.misconception: A protein is just one amino acid repeated over and over.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Addition polymers use a single repeating unit, so that pattern is assumed to hold for every polymer.
misconceptions.correction: Proteins are built by combining different amino acids in one chain, which is what gives each protein its own properties.

misconceptions.question: How many polymer chains are there in most DNA molecules?
misconceptions.correct: Two, twisted into a double helix.
misconceptions.misconception: DNA is a single chain that coils round to give a double helix.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Double' is read as describing the coiling of one strand rather than the number of strands.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: most DNA molecules are two polymer chains in the form of a double helix.

misconceptions.question: What are the monomers of DNA?
misconceptions.correct: Four different monomers called nucleotides.
misconceptions.misconception: DNA is made from amino acids, like proteins are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: DNA and proteins are both biological polymers met together, so their monomers get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Amino acids build proteins. DNA is built from four different nucleotides.

misconceptions.question: How many different nucleotides build DNA?
misconceptions.correct: Four.
misconceptions.misconception: There are two different nucleotides, one for each chain.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The double helix has two strands, and that number is transferred to the number of monomers.
misconceptions.correction: There are four different nucleotides; the two chains are made from the same set of four.

misconceptions.question: Which monomer builds starch and cellulose?
misconceptions.correct: Glucose.
misconceptions.misconception: Starch and cellulose are built from amino acids.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Amino acid is the biological monomer students recall most readily, so it is offered for every natural polymer.
misconceptions.correction: Both starch and cellulose are polymers of glucose; amino acids build proteins instead.

misconceptions.question: Is glucose a polymer?
misconceptions.correct: No. Glucose is a monomer.
misconceptions.misconception: Glucose belongs in a list of naturally occurring polymers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Glucose is met alongside starch and cellulose in biology, so it is grouped with them without checking the size.
misconceptions.correction: Glucose is a small molecule and is the monomer; starch and cellulose are the polymers made from it.

misconceptions.question: Is DNA a polymer?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, and most DNA molecules are two polymer chains.
misconceptions.misconception: DNA is not a polymer because polymers are man-made plastics.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Polymers are introduced through poly(ethene) and plastics, so 'polymer' becomes a synonym for a synthetic material.
misconceptions.correction: A polymer is any very large molecule built from many monomers, whether it is made in a factory or in a cell.

misconceptions.question: Is any small molecule lost when chloroethene polymerises?
misconceptions.correct: No. Addition polymerisation forms no other product.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen chloride is given off when chloroethene polymerises.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A chlorine atom is visible in the formula, so students expect it to be lost as HCl in the way water is lost elsewhere.
misconceptions.correction: The chlorine stays on the chain. Addition polymerisation joins the monomers with no other molecule formed.

misconceptions.question: Does an addition polymer contain every atom from its monomers?
misconceptions.correct: Yes, all of them.
misconceptions.misconception: Some atoms are lost as a small molecule when the chain forms.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Chain-forming is imagined as requiring atoms to be removed, as in condensation polymerisation.
misconceptions.correction: Because no other molecule is formed, the mass of polymer equals the mass of monomer used.

misconceptions.question: What is cellulose made from?
misconceptions.correct: Glucose monomers.
misconceptions.misconception: Cellulose is a polymer made by joining starch molecules together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Starch and cellulose are met as a pair, so one is assumed to be built from the other.
misconceptions.correction: Starch and cellulose are two different polymers, each built directly from glucose monomers.

misconceptions.question: Why is DNA described as having four different monomers?
misconceptions.correct: Because four different nucleotides are used to build the chains.
misconceptions.misconception: There is one polymer chain for each of the four nucleotides.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The words 'four' and 'two' both appear in the description, so the numbers are attached to the wrong things.
misconceptions.correction: Most DNA molecules have two chains, and each chain is built from a sequence of the four different nucleotides.

misconceptions.question: Does a polyester form from one monomer or two?
misconceptions.correct: Two different monomers, alternating along the chain.
misconceptions.misconception: Many ethanediol molecules join to each other to form the polyester.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Addition polymers use a single monomer, so the same picture is applied to condensation polymers.
misconceptions.correction: An ester link needs an –OH group and a –COOH group, so the diol and the diacid must alternate along the chain.

misconceptions.question: Which functional group shows a molecule can be an addition monomer?
misconceptions.correct: The C=C carbon–carbon double bond.
misconceptions.misconception: An –OH group at the end of the molecule shows it can polymerise by addition.
misconceptions.whyItArises: –OH is the functional group most recently learned in organic chemistry, so it is offered as the reactive group.
misconceptions.correction: For addition polymerisation the required functional group is C=C. An –OH group belongs to alcohols and to condensation monomers.

misconceptions.question: Does the repeating unit of a condensation polymer contain every atom of the monomers?
misconceptions.correct: No. The atoms that leave as water are missing from the repeating unit.
misconceptions.misconception: The repeating unit keeps all the atoms of the monomers, including the full –OH, –COOH or –NH₂ groups.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule that the repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer is learned for addition polymers and then applied to condensation polymers as well.
misconceptions.correction: That rule holds only when no other molecule is formed. In condensation polymerisation water is lost at every link, so those atoms are not in the repeating unit.

mcqs.stem: Poly(ethene) and poly(propene) are made by addition polymerisation. Why are alkenes, rather than alkanes, used as the monomers?

options.text: Alkenes contain a C=C bond that can open to make new bonds
options.rationale: The specification states that alkenes are used to make addition polymers; the C=C is the group that opens so each monomer can bond to two neighbours.

options.text: Alkanes are saturated, so their molecules join end to end
options.rationale: 'Saturated' is read as meaning full and ready to combine, rather than as having no double bond to open.

options.text: Alkene molecules are held by weak intermolecular forces
options.rationale: Intermolecular forces are used to explain polymer properties, so students use them to explain chain formation too.

options.text: Ethane is used, since poly(ethene) is named after it
options.rationale: 'Ethene' and 'ethane' sound almost identical, so the more familiar alkane name is chosen.

mcqs.stem: Which monomer is used to make poly(propene)?

options.text: Propane, because the polymer chain is completely saturated
options.rationale: The finished chain really is saturated, so students work backwards to a saturated starting material.

options.text: Propene, because its molecules contain a C=C double bond
options.rationale: Poly(propene) is the addition polymer of propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, named after the alkene monomer used.

options.text: Ethene, because three ethene units give a propene unit
options.rationale: The 'prop' prefix is treated as a count of smaller units rather than as three carbons in one monomer.

options.text: Propanol, because poly(propene) is named from –OH
options.rationale: –OH is the most recently learned functional group, so it is offered as the reactive group.

mcqs.stem: What happens to the molecules in an addition polymerisation reaction?

options.text: One monomer molecule grows by taking in more atoms
options.rationale: Growth is imagined as one molecule swelling rather than as thousands of separate molecules linking.

options.text: Many monomers join and water molecules are given off
options.rationale: Water loss is the memorable feature of condensation polymerisation and gets attached to both types.

options.text: Many small monomers join into one large molecule
options.rationale: The specification says many small molecules (monomers) join together to form very large molecules (polymers).

options.text: One large molecule splits into small monomers
options.rationale: The arrow is read in reverse, and cracking of long chains is a recent and similar-looking idea.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about a sample of poly(ethene) is correct?

options.text: Every chain holds the same number of units
options.rationale: Chemical formulae usually describe one fixed molecule, so a fixed chain length is expected.

options.text: The units in a chain are held by weak forces
options.rationale: Intermolecular forces between chains are confused with the bonds inside a chain.

options.text: Each chain contains two joined ethene molecules
options.rationale: n is read as a small whole number in the way balancing numbers usually are.

options.text: The chains are of many different lengths
options.rationale: n is not a fixed number: a sample contains chains built from different numbers of repeating units.

mcqs.stem: The specification gives the example n CH₂=CH₂ → –(CH₂–CH₂)–n . What does this equation tell you?

options.text: n ethene molecules give one chain of n repeating units
options.rationale: The same symbol n appears on both sides: every monomer molecule that reacts becomes one repeating unit in the chain.

options.text: n ethene molecules give a polymer and n waters
options.rationale: Loss of water from condensation polymerisation is transferred to addition polymerisation.

options.text: Two ethene molecules give a chain two units long
options.rationale: The letter n is read as standing for a small definite number such as two.

options.text: n ethene molecules give a chain that still has C=C
options.rationale: The monomer is copied into the brackets unchanged, because the atoms present do not change.

mcqs.stem: The repeating unit of poly(ethene) is –CH₂–CH₂–. Why does it contain the same atoms as the ethene monomer?

options.text: Because the water that is lost is later taken back in
options.rationale: Students who expect water loss invent a step that returns the atoms so the formula still matches.

options.text: Because no other molecule is formed in this reaction
options.rationale: This is the reason the specification gives: nothing else is produced, so every atom of the monomer stays in the repeating unit.

options.text: Because two hydrogen atoms are lost from each end
options.rationale: Joining molecules is assumed to cost atoms, by analogy with condensation reactions.

options.text: Because the C=C double bond is kept in the chain
options.rationale: 'Same atoms' is read as 'same structure', so the double bond is kept as well.

mcqs.stem: 500 g of ethene is completely polymerised. Which statement about the atoms involved is correct?

options.text: Some atoms leave because a small molecule is released
options.rationale: Chain formation is pictured as requiring atoms to be removed, as happens in condensation polymerisation.

options.text: The polymer holds more carbon atoms per hydrogen
options.rationale: The polymer is thought to lose hydrogen as the chain forms, changing the ratio of atoms.

options.text: All the atoms end up in the poly(ethene) formed
options.rationale: No other molecule is formed, so every atom from the ethene is in the polymer and 500 g of poly(ethene) is produced.

options.text: One hydrogen per monomer ends off the chain
options.rationale: The ends of the chain are over-thought, and a hydrogen is invented to cap them.

mcqs.stem: Which feature of a molecule shows that it can be a monomer for addition polymerisation?

options.text: An –OH group on an end carbon
options.rationale: –OH is the functional group most recently met, so it is assumed to be the reactive one.

options.text: A long, unbranched carbon chain
options.rationale: Polymers look like long chains, so a long monomer is assumed to be needed to make one.

options.text: Two –COOH groups, one at each end
options.rationale: The condensation rule of two functional groups is applied to addition polymerisation.

options.text: A carbon–carbon double bond
options.rationale: The specification asks students to recognise monomers from the presence of the functional group C=C.

mcqs.stem: Which description is of an addition polymer rather than of a monomer?

options.text: A repeating unit in brackets with no bonds crossing them
options.rationale: Brackets are treated as closing off a finished molecule, so the extension bonds are left out.

options.text: A short molecule that holds just one C=C double bond
options.rationale: The C=C is remembered as the polymer's key feature rather than the monomer's.

options.text: A repeating unit in brackets with bonds through them and n
options.rationale: The specification's form for a polymer is the repeating unit in brackets, with extension bonds through the brackets and n outside.

options.text: A long molecule with an –OH group at each of its ends
options.rationale: A molecule with two functional groups is assumed to be an addition polymer.

mcqs.stem: Chloroethene is CH₂=CHCl. Which description of the equation for its polymerisation is correct?

options.text: n CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets plus n HCl given off
options.rationale: The visible chlorine atom is expected to leave, in the way water leaves a condensation reaction.

options.text: n CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets keeping the C=C
options.rationale: The monomer is copied into the brackets without opening the double bond.

options.text: Two CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets with a 2 shown
options.rationale: n is replaced by a small number because balancing numbers are usually small.

options.text: n CH₂=CHCl on the left, brackets with n on the right
options.rationale: n monomer molecules give a chain of n repeating units, –(CH₂–CHCl)–n, with no other product.

mcqs.stem: When the repeating unit of an addition polymer is drawn, why are bonds drawn through the brackets?

options.text: To show more units are joined on both sides of it
options.rationale: The extension bonds show that the unit is one link in a long chain, not a separate molecule.

options.text: To show the unit is a complete and separate molecule
options.rationale: Brackets are normally used to close off a group, so they are read as ending the molecule.

options.text: To show where the double bond once was in the monomer
options.rationale: The bonds are read as leftovers of the C=C rather than as links to neighbours.

options.text: To show the point at which each chain stops
options.rationale: A fixed chain length is assumed, so the bonds are read as end markers.

mcqs.stem: The repeating unit of a polymer is –CH₂–CH(CH₃)–. Which molecule was the monomer?

options.text: Propane, as all bonds are single
options.rationale: The repeating unit contains only single bonds, so a saturated monomer is chosen.

options.text: Propene, since the C=C re-forms
options.rationale: The repeating unit has three carbons; putting the double bond back between the two chain carbons gives propene, CH₃CH=CH₂.

options.text: Butene, as the unit has 4 carbons
options.rationale: The branch carbon is counted twice, or the atoms are miscounted from the brackets.

options.text: Ethene plus methane, as it branches
options.rationale: The branch is treated as a separate small molecule that joined on.

mcqs.stem: Tetrafluoroethene, CF₂=CF₂, undergoes addition polymerisation. What is the repeating unit of the polymer?

options.text: –CF₂=CF₂– with the double bond still in place
options.rationale: The monomer is copied straight into the brackets without opening the double bond.

options.text: –CF₂–CF₂– without bonds through the brackets
options.rationale: The extension bonds are omitted because brackets are read as closing the unit.

options.text: –CF₂–CF₂– with the bonds drawn through the brackets
options.rationale: The C=C opens to a single bond, the atoms are unchanged, and extension bonds show the unit joining on both sides.

options.text: –CF₂–CF₂– after two fluorine atoms are lost
options.rationale: Atoms are assumed to be lost when monomers join.

mcqs.stem: What must a monomer have in order to take part in condensation polymerisation?

options.text: A carbon–carbon double bond in each of the monomers
options.rationale: The C=C rule for addition polymerisation is carried over to every kind of polymerisation.

options.text: One functional group at one end of a chain
options.rationale: A single reaction between two molecules is pictured, not a chain that must grow at both ends.

options.text: A boiling point low enough for it to condense
options.rationale: The everyday meaning of condensation is applied to the name of the reaction.

options.text: Two functional groups in each monomer molecule
options.rationale: The specification states that condensation polymerisation involves monomers with two functional groups.

mcqs.stem: Why is this type of polymerisation called condensation polymerisation?

options.text: A small molecule such as water is lost each time
options.rationale: The specification says the monomers join together, usually losing small molecules such as water, and so the reactions are called condensation reactions.

options.text: A gas condenses to a liquid as the polymer is made
options.rationale: The weather and windows meaning of condensation is far more familiar than the chemical one.

options.text: The monomer solution becomes much more concentrated
options.rationale: 'Condensed' is read as concentrated, which is another everyday sense of the word.

options.text: Carbon dioxide gas is given off as chains grow
options.rationale: Acids are associated with releasing carbon dioxide, so that product is recalled.

mcqs.stem: The simplest condensation polymers are made from two different monomers. What is true of those two monomers?

options.text: Each carries two different groups
options.rationale: This is true of amino acids, which polymerise alone, so it is misapplied to the two-monomer case.

options.text: Each has two of the same group
options.rationale: The specification states that the simplest polymers come from two different monomers with two of the same functional groups on each monomer.

options.text: Each carries one group at an end
options.rationale: One functional group per monomer is thought to be enough to build a chain.

options.text: Each carries a C=C and an –OH group
options.rationale: The addition polymerisation requirement for C=C is added to the condensation requirement.

mcqs.stem: Ethanediol and hexanedioic acid are heated together. Which statement describes the polymerisation?

options.text: Many ethanediol molecules join each other, losing water
options.rationale: The single-monomer picture from addition polymerisation is applied to a polyester.

options.text: The two monomers join with no other product formed
options.rationale: Addition polymerisation, in which nothing else is formed, is applied to a condensation reaction.

options.text: The two different monomers join alternately, losing water
options.rationale: An ester link needs an –OH group and a –COOH group, so the diol and the diacid alternate, releasing water at each link.

options.text: The two monomers join and carbon dioxide is given off
options.rationale: The presence of an acid suggests carbon dioxide, as in reactions with carbonates.

mcqs.stem: Which description of the monomer ethanediol is correct?

options.text: Two carbon atoms, with a single –OH group on it
options.rationale: Ethanol is met first and looks similar, so only one –OH group is expected.

options.text: Two carbon atoms, with a –COOH at each end
options.rationale: The two monomers of the polyester are swapped, and the acid groups given to the diol.

options.text: Two carbons joined by a C=C double bond
options.rationale: The C=C requirement from addition polymerisation is carried over.

options.text: Two carbon atoms, with an –OH group on each
options.rationale: Ethanediol is HOCH₂CH₂OH: 'eth' gives two carbons and 'diol' gives two –OH groups.

mcqs.stem: Hexanedioic acid is the second monomer used to make this polyester. Which description of it is correct?

options.text: Six carbon atoms, with a –COOH group at each end
options.rationale: Hexanedioic acid is HOOC(CH₂)₄COOH: 'hexane' gives six carbons and 'dioic acid' gives two –COOH groups.

options.text: Six carbon atoms, with just one –COOH group on an end
options.rationale: Carboxylic acids are first met as one-ended molecules such as ethanoic acid.

options.text: Six carbon atoms, with an –OH group at either end
options.rationale: The two monomers are swapped and the alcohol groups given to the acid.

options.text: Six carbon atoms, with a –COOH and an –NH₂ end
options.rationale: The amino acid pattern of two different groups is applied to this monomer.

mcqs.stem: What is produced when ethanediol and hexanedioic acid polymerise together?

options.text: A polyester and no other product
options.rationale: Addition polymerisation, which forms no other product, is applied to a condensation reaction.

options.text: A polyester and water molecules
options.rationale: The –OH and –COOH groups react to form ester links along the chain, releasing a molecule of water at each link.

options.text: A polypeptide and water molecules
options.rationale: Both are condensation polymers, so the two product names are swapped.

options.text: A polyester and carbon dioxide gas
options.rationale: The acid monomer suggests carbon dioxide as the gas released.

mcqs.stem: Amino acids can polymerise on their own, without a second kind of monomer. Why is this possible?

options.text: Each molecule has two of the same functional group
options.rationale: The rule learned for polyesters, two of the same group per monomer, is applied to amino acids.

options.text: Each molecule has a carbon–carbon double bond
options.rationale: The C=C requirement from addition polymerisation is carried over.

options.text: Each molecule carries two different functional groups
options.rationale: The specification states that amino acids have two different functional groups in a molecule, an –NH₂ and a –COOH, so one monomer can link at both ends.

options.text: Each molecule carries one group that reacts twice
options.rationale: One functional group is thought to be enough if it reacts more than once.

mcqs.stem: Glycine is H₂NCH₂COOH. Which groups react when glycine molecules polymerise, and what is lost?

options.text: –NH₂ with –COOH, losing one ammonia molecule
options.rationale: The nitrogen in –NH₂ is expected to leave with the small molecule.

options.text: Two –COOH groups, losing a water molecule
options.rationale: The polyester pattern of two identical groups is applied to glycine.

options.text: C=C with –COOH, losing a water molecule
options.rationale: A C=C is assumed to be needed for any polymerisation.

options.text: –NH₂ with –COOH, losing one water molecule
options.rationale: The two different groups on neighbouring molecules react together, and H from –NH₂ with OH from –COOH leaves as water.

mcqs.stem: How does a protein differ from a polypeptide made from a single kind of amino acid?

options.text: Different amino acids are combined in one chain
options.rationale: The specification states that different amino acids can be combined in the same chain to produce proteins.

options.text: The same amino acid is repeated along the whole chain
options.rationale: The single repeating unit of an addition polymer is assumed to apply to every polymer.

options.text: Two separate chains are twisted round each other
options.rationale: The double helix of DNA is transferred to proteins.

options.text: Whole polypeptides act as the monomers used
options.rationale: The polymer is thought to be built from smaller polymers rather than from amino acids.

mcqs.stem: Why is DNA described as essential for life?

options.text: It is a store of energy in cells
options.rationale: Starch is an energy store and is met alongside DNA, so the roles are swapped.

options.text: It encodes genetic instructions
options.rationale: The specification states that DNA encodes genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms and viruses.

options.text: It supplies the amino acids needed
options.rationale: DNA is linked with proteins, so it is assumed to supply their monomers.

options.text: It is a protein that speeds reactions
options.rationale: DNA and proteins are both biological polymers and their identities get confused.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the structure of most DNA molecules?

options.text: One polymer chain coiled into a double helix
options.rationale: 'Double' is read as describing how one strand coils rather than the number of strands.

options.text: Four polymer chains, one per type of nucleotide
options.rationale: The number four, which refers to the nucleotides, is attached to the chains instead.

options.text: Two polymer chains in the form of a double helix
options.rationale: The specification states that most DNA molecules are two polymer chains in the form of a double helix.

options.text: Two chains, each built from two nucleotides
options.rationale: The two strands of the helix are matched one-to-one with the number of different nucleotides.

mcqs.stem: Which list contains only naturally occurring polymers?

options.text: DNA, proteins, starch and poly(ethene)
options.rationale: Poly(ethene) is the polymer students know best, so it is included without checking its origin.

options.text: DNA, glucose, starch and cellulose
options.rationale: Glucose is met alongside starch and cellulose, so it is grouped with them.

options.text: DNA, proteins, glucose and starch
options.rationale: Monomers are listed among polymers because they appear in the same topic.

options.text: DNA, proteins, starch and cellulose
options.rationale: These are the naturally occurring polymers important for life that the specification names.

mcqs.stem: Name the type of monomer from which both starch and cellulose are made.

options.text: Glucose molecules build both these polymers
options.rationale: Starch and cellulose are both naturally occurring polymers of glucose.

options.text: Amino acids build both of these long polymers
options.rationale: Amino acid is the biological monomer recalled most readily, so it is offered for every natural polymer.

options.text: Starch molecules join together to make cellulose
options.rationale: The two are met as a pair, so one is assumed to be built from the other.

options.text: Nucleotides build both of these polymers
options.rationale: Nucleotides are the other named biological monomer and get attached to the wrong polymer.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly matches these naturally occurring polymers to their monomers?

options.text: Proteins from nucleotides; DNA from the amino acids
options.rationale: The two biological monomers are met together and get swapped between the polymers.

options.text: Proteins from amino acids; DNA from nucleotides
options.rationale: Proteins are polymers of amino acids and DNA is built from four different nucleotides.

options.text: Proteins from amino acids; DNA from glucose units
options.rationale: Glucose is offered because it is the other monomer named in the topic.

options.text: Proteins from glucose; DNA from the four nucleotides
options.rationale: Glucose is treated as a general biological building block for all natural polymers.

mcqs.stem: Ethanediol and hexanedioic acid polymerise. What is shown in the repeating unit of the polymer formed?

options.text: An ester link, with bonds drawn through the brackets
options.rationale: An –OH group and a –COOH group react to give an ester link, and the extension bonds show the unit repeating along the chain.

options.text: An ester link, with the brackets closed off
options.rationale: Brackets are read as closing off a finished molecule, so the extension bonds are left out.

options.text: A peptide link joining the two monomer units
options.rationale: Polyesters and polypeptides are both condensation polymers, so their links get swapped.

options.text: Two ethanediol units joined to one another
options.rationale: The single-monomer picture from addition polymerisation is applied to a polyester.

mcqs.stem: Glycine, H₂NCH₂COOH, polymerises to make a polypeptide. What is the repeating unit of that polypeptide?

options.text: –NH₂–CH₂–COOH– with bonds through the brackets
options.rationale: The addition polymer rule that no atoms are lost is applied here, so the whole monomer is kept.

options.text: –NH–CH₂–CO– with bonds through the brackets
options.rationale: The H lost from –NH₂ and the OH lost from –COOH leave as water, so –NH–CH₂–CO– repeats along the chain.

options.text: –O–CH₂–CO– with bonds through the brackets
options.rationale: The ester link of a polyester is used, so the nitrogen is replaced by an oxygen in the chain.

options.text: –CH₂–CO– with bonds through the brackets
options.rationale: The nitrogen is expected to leave as ammonia, so it is missing from the unit.
